title: Apply basic human resource management principles and practices applicable in an agricultural environment

lessons.title: Workplace rules and the labour laws
lessons.html:
What is human resource management?

Human resource management (HR) is how a farm looks after its people: hiring, pay, leave, rules, safety, training and records. Every farm should have clear rules so that everyone knows what is expected and is treated fairly.

Rules and procedures on the farm

  • Working hours: when you start, when you take breaks and when you finish.
  • Reporting absence: if you are sick or cannot come to work, tell your supervisor as early as you can.
  • Disciplinary procedure: the steps followed when someone breaks a rule, such as a verbal warning, a written warning and a hearing. You have the right to tell your side of the story.
  • Grievance procedure: the steps you follow if you have a complaint about your work or how you are treated. Usually you first speak to your supervisor, and if that does not help you go to the next manager.

Labour laws that protect farm workers

LawWhat it covers
Basic Conditions of Employment Act 75 of 1997Working hours, overtime, leave, payslips
Sectoral Determination for Farm WorkersExtra rules for the farm sector
National Minimum Wage Act 9 of 2018The lowest wage that may be paid
Labour Relations Act 66 of 1995Fair dismissal, unions, disputes (CCMA)
Employment Equity Act 55 of 1998No unfair discrimination
Occupational Health and Safety Act 85 of 1993A safe workplace
Compensation for Occupational Injuries and Diseases Act 130 of 1993Pay and care if you are injured at work
Unemployment Insurance Act 63 of 2001UIF payments if you lose your job

You do not need to know every detail. You must know that these laws exist, and where to ask: your supervisor, the farm office, or the Department of Employment and Labour.

lessons.title: Contracts and benefits
lessons.html:
Your employment contract

When you start work, you should get the main terms of your job in writing. This shows your name, job, start date, working hours, wage, how often you are paid and your leave.

Types of contracts and agreements

  • Permanent contract: no end date. You work until you resign, retire or are fairly dismissed.
  • Fixed-term contract: for a set time, for example six months.
  • Seasonal contract: for a season, such as the harvest or pruning season.
  • Casual or day work: for a short job.
  • Collective agreement: an agreement between the employer and a trade union about pay and conditions for a group of workers.
  • Housing agreement: if you live on the farm, there may be a separate agreement about the house.

Read your contract or ask someone to read it to you. Do not sign anything you do not understand. Keep your copy safe.

Benefits at work

A benefit is something you receive from your work besides your wage. Some are required by law and some depend on the farm.

  • Annual leave: paid holiday every year.
  • Sick leave: paid days when you are ill, usually with a doctor's note if you are away longer.
  • Family responsibility leave and maternity leave.
  • UIF: you and the employer both pay a small amount each month.
  • COIDA: covers you if you are injured at work.
  • Farm benefits such as housing, transport, protective clothing, a pension or provident fund, or medical aid.

Your payslip shows your wage and every deduction. Check it every pay day and ask the farm office if something looks wrong.

lessons.title: Health and safety rules and HR records
lessons.html:
Health and safety at work

The Occupational Health and Safety Act 85 of 1993 says the employer must make the workplace safe, and workers must also work safely. Your duties are:

  • Follow the safety rules and instructions.
  • Wear the protective clothing (PPE) you are given, such as boots, gloves and masks.
  • Use machines and tools only if you are trained to use them.
  • Report any unsafe situation and every injury, even a small one, to your supervisor.
  • Never work under the influence of alcohol or drugs.

You may refuse to do work that is clearly dangerous to your life, but tell your supervisor or health and safety representative at once.

Human resource records

The farm keeps records about every worker. These include:

  • contracts and personal details (ID number, address, next of kin),
  • attendance registers and clock cards,
  • leave forms,
  • wage records and payslips,
  • training certificates,
  • injury reports and disciplinary records.

Filing records properly

  1. Put each document in the right worker's file, usually filed by surname or employee number.
  2. Write clearly and date every form.
  3. Keep files in a locked cabinet or a password-protected computer. Personal information is private and is protected by law (the Protection of Personal Information Act).
  4. Do not take files home or show them to other workers.
  5. Return a file to its place as soon as you are done.

Good records help you too: they prove how much leave you have, what you were paid and what training you have done.

Key points

  • Know the farm's rules, disciplinary and grievance procedures.
  • Labour laws such as the BCEA, LRA, OHS Act and COIDA protect farm workers.
  • Get your contract in writing and do not sign what you do not understand.
  • Check your payslip and know your leave and other benefits.
  • Keep HR records accurate, filed correctly and private.
